newsitem.title: THAILAND: SE Asia Grain - Thais in corn, soybean buying spree.
newsitem.headline: SE Asia Grain - Thais in corn, soybean buying spree.

text.p: Thailand has gone on a buying spree picking up 38,000 tonnes of corn from Argentina and 50,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans, traders said on Wednesday.
The Thais may also be in the market for another 50,000 tonnes of soybeans and 20,000 tonnes of soymeal, they added.

Thanakorn Vegetable Oil, one of Thailand's major oil crushers, bought 50,000 tonnes of soybeans from Brazil for May delivery while another crusher, Thai Vegetable Oil, was likewise seeking 50,000 tonnes of beans for June shipment.
Thai Vegetable Oil is expected to clinch the deal soon.
A slide in Chicago futures prices may tempt more buyers in Thailand to step into the market.
"We expect to secure more orders as prices dip," one dealer in Bangkok said.

Prices of local soymeal reached 10.30 baht a kg while locally-crushed imported beans also firmed to 9.90 baht a kg from 9.70-9.80 baht last week. Corn prices inched up to 4.60-4.65 baht a kg from the previous week's 4.50-4.60 baht.
In Indonesia, corn prices were under pressure from players seeking to sell their imported cargoes, even as 50,000 tonnes of Chinese corn was set to arrive, traders said.

"Corn prices are weaker because the big players are selling hard because their Chinese corn can match the price of local corn," one trader said. "Two feedmills are expected to take delivery of about 50,000 tonnes of Chinese corn at end-April."

The trader said Chinese corn was on offer at around US$150 a tonne C&F, compared with $157 a tonne C&F for U.S. corn on a Panamax. "Last week, one feedmill took delivery of about 20,000 tonnes of Chinese corn," a dealer said.
He said buyers were showing little interest in U.S. corn in the wake of cheaper offers from China.
Traders said the selling pressure had forced local corn prices to ease to 400 rupiah a kg in Jakarta from 405-410 rupiah a week ago. They expected prices to slip further.
"There are many players selling imported corn," another trader said. "It would be difficult for farmers if prices go down further because they get about only 300 rupiah a kg."
"But fortunately, the prices of cash crops such as tapioca are also low so they might not switch crops for now," she said.

Soymeal prices, however, were rising on the back of strong demand, climbing to 860-870 rupiah a kg in Jakarta from 830-840 rupiah last week, dealers said. One trader said Indian soymeal was being offered at $340-$345 a tonne C&F.
"The soymeal market is strong, and I expect it to remain steady through next week," the trader said.
The Malaysian grains and oilseeds market was quiet the whole of the past week, with consumers having ample coverage for their nearby needs, trade sources said.
"If it's corn, especially, I think we've more than what we need in the immediate future," said the purchasing manager of a flour mill in Kuala Lumpur.
Bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, was seen at 410 ringgit tonne C&F, compared to 420-430 ringgit a week earlier.
Traders said the price could go down further next week as the market was saturated.
"For now, most importers have a stockpile of up to two to three months," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur. "So if we're looking at the next major buys, we're talking about June/July."
Another trader said importers could still lock in orders for forward months if prices fell sharply in coming weeks.
Local soymeal was seen at 880 ringgit while imported soymeal was quoted at 870 ringgit.
Grade A wheat was quoted at 750-800 ringgit a tonne while "B" grade wheat fetched a quote of 450 ringgit per tonne.
